thesis: Games use regular updates to keep movement going and events to react to discrete changes.
example: A jump tap is saved for the next physics step, while a pressure plate tells the door when someone steps on it.
fit: You want a beginner-friendly explanation of game loops and events using familiar controls.

thesis: A game can keep its health rules in one component and let signals update the interface and effects.
example: The health component applies a hit and then sends the new total to the health bar and animation.
fit: You want to explain signals, ownership of state, and how game systems stay independent.

thesis: An event queue lets a game choose when to handle a burst of work, but the team needs a policy for full queues and delayed messages.
example: Five impacts arrive together. The sound system can combine their requests while keeping important player feedback.
fit: You want a technical presentation on queues, priority and responsiveness.

thesis: A game gets more predictable when one controller resolves conflicting events before announcing an outcome.
example: A player reaches a checkpoint and a hazard in the same step. The controller consistently gives the hazard priority.
fit: You want one clear timing bug to explain and a repeatable test to demonstrate.

thesis: A game's update loop, state changes and notifications each have different jobs. Dividing them clearly makes rules easier to test.
example: A player collects a key and presses interact in one step. The game records the pickup first, then decides whether to open the exit.
fit: You want to explain how events and the game loop work together through one complete example.

thesis: Objects work best when their methods protect rules that belong with their state.
example: The library website and the desk use the same renewal method, so both apply the same due-date rule.
fit: You want a gentle introduction to classes, methods and encapsulation.

thesis: Encapsulation keeps an object valid when other parts of the application request changes.
example: An old browser page tries to renew a returned book. The loan refuses and preserves the saved dates.
fit: You want a concrete example of how an object protects its own state.

thesis: Composition is useful when a rule changes independently of the object that uses it.
example: The same lending service can use one-week or three-week renewal policies without creating a subclass for each case.
fit: You want to weigh inheritance, composition and straightforward functions in one design.

thesis: The structure of a program should follow the job each part does.
example: A loan object protects a return operation. A query counts monthly returns by category.
fit: You want to explain when a class adds clarity and when a query or function is sufficient.

thesis: An object can enforce local rules, while a service and database coordinate rules involving several records.
example: A reservation and renewal arrive together, so the service has to coordinate both requests against current records.
fit: You want the strongest object-oriented design discussion and feel comfortable explaining transactions.

thesis: Repeatable tests turn requirements into specific checks and help catch regressions.
example: Delivery adds to the total but does not count towards the £50 discount threshold.
fit: You want a straightforward introduction to unit, integration and checkout tests.

thesis: A test is most revealing where a rule changes its answer.
example: Baskets at £49.99, £50.00 and £50.01 expose a mistake in an inclusive threshold.
fit: You want a short, interactive demo with numbers the audience can check by hand.

thesis: Reliability depends on what happens between parts of a system as well as inside each part.
example: A rejected checkout must leave consistent order and stock records, which a test checks in the database.
fit: You want to discuss integration tests, real storage and recovery from failure.

thesis: Automated results are useful when the starting conditions can be reproduced.
example: A test feeds the same time into an offer that expires at midnight, so the result does not depend on the real clock.
fit: You want a focused talk on flaky tests and continuous integration.

thesis: Testing works best when each check targets a specific risk.
example: A discount release uses a unit test for price, an integration test for the saved order and a checkout test for the receipt.
fit: You want a balanced software engineering essay that explains what each level of testing can prove.

thesis: AI hints can help beginners move forward while still giving them a step to work out themselves.
example: A student asks about the running total and then writes and checks the program that computes the average.
fit: You want a simple explanation of how a hint can support a beginner.

thesis: An AI suggestion becomes a useful learning exercise when the student checks it against the requirement.
example: Dividing the sum by the count works for a normal list and fails on an empty one. The student tests and fixes that case.
fit: You want a small coding demonstration with a precise before-and-after result.

thesis: Finishing an exercise and applying the skill independently later provide different evidence about learning.
example: A class records performance with AI hints, then asks students to average a subset of scores without help.
fit: You want to discuss how to measure learning and what the research can establish.

thesis: A fair course gives students several ways to get help while protecting their data.
example: Students use invented scores when asking for help and can use an equivalent written hint.
fit: You want to focus on privacy and access to AI support.

thesis: AI can help during practice, and a separate task can demonstrate what each learner can do independently.
example: Learners try, test and explain an average function with optional hints before tackling a related problem alone.
fit: You want to use classroom research to argue for a concrete teaching and assessment approach.

thesis: Essential clues are easier to use when colour, words and shapes carry the same information.
example: A red or green door light gains a lock icon and a Ready or Locked label.
fit: You want a quick before-and-after design demonstration with a clear visual point.

thesis: A caption needs to convey the meaning of an important game sound in time for the player to act.
example: A west-door alarm gets a caption, a direction marker and a countdown for players with the sound off.
fit: You want to demonstrate one accessibility feature clearly and explain the design choices behind it.

thesis: Remapping and input alternatives can make game actions easier to perform while preserving the puzzle.
example: A player can tap to grip and release a valve instead of holding a control while turning it.
fit: You want to discuss input access, timing and the difference between puzzle difficulty and control difficulty.

thesis: Accessibility settings help only when players can find them, change them and confirm that they work.
example: A keyboard user adjusts text size and then checks that the tutorial uses the new setting.
fit: You want to focus on keyboard navigation, focus and spoken feedback.

thesis: Accessibility works across the whole player journey, from finding settings to understanding the result of an action.
example: A player enlarges text, remaps a button and turns on captions, then uses all three settings to follow a station alarm and open the right door.
fit: You want a visual example that covers several accessibility decisions in one demonstration.

thesis: Fair purchases show the actual price and make it clear when a player has agreed to pay.
example: A £4.99 outfit is compared with the same outfit sold through a bundle of game credits.
fit: You want a relatable presentation about prices, consent and confusing shop interfaces.

thesis: A loot box has a known price per purchase and an uncertain cost for getting the item a player wants.
example: Ten £2 attempts at a fixed 2% chance give about an 18% chance of getting the outfit at least once, assuming independent draws.
fit: You want an ethics topic with a memorable numerical example and a reason to distinguish association from causation.

thesis: Family purchase permissions and children's privacy need to be designed together.
example: A child profile blocks paid random purchases until an adult approves, using only the information required to apply the setting.
fit: You want to focus on younger players, family controls and data minimisation.

thesis: A survey about gambling risk and a test of a purchase screen answer different questions.
example: The studio tests whether players can identify the cost and cancel, while survey evidence helps it assess broader risk.
fit: You want to compare evidence and defend a recommendation without overstating what the research proves.

thesis: Consent depends on the entire purchase journey, including cost, confirmation, receipts and support.
example: A shopper compares the odds, can cancel before paying, and gets a clear receipt if they buy.
fit: You want a broad ethics argument organised around one complete purchase.

thesis: Python makes it easy to teach lists and loops with data that beginners can check by hand.
example: A reading log goes from 12 to 12 to 30 minutes as the program adds each entry.
fit: You want the most approachable introduction to Python.

thesis: A short Python exercise can connect a condition, a loop and a boundary case.
example: A reading log counts two days at or above 15 minutes, including the day at exactly 15.
fit: You want an audience-friendly demonstration of how conditions and loops interact.

thesis: A trace turns an incorrect result into evidence about which line needs to change.
example: A reading log returns 18 instead of 30 because it resets the total on every pass through the loop.
fit: You want a live debugging demo the audience can solve with you.

thesis: Beginner input exercises can teach the difference between converting text and checking its meaning.
example: The word fifteen fails conversion. A negative integer converts successfully but is invalid for reading minutes.
fit: You want to explain useful error messages, types and input validation.

thesis: A good first Python course teaches reasoning habits that carry over to new tasks.
example: A learner adapts a reading log to count practice sessions, then changes it to total the qualifying minutes.
fit: You want to discuss how beginners transfer a skill across problems and languages.
